title: The Assumption of Mary: Putting Our Hand in Hers2
opening: Lord, meet us gently today and always
body:
Today we celebrate the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary, the woman who believed before so many of us knew how to believe. Mary is our guide, the first among believers, and a mother whose heart would be pierced through her love for her Son and her witness to His suffering.

Everything began with her yes. When the angel came to Mary, she could not possibly have understood everything her answer would require of her. Yet she responded, "Behold, I am the handmaid of the Lord. May it be done to me according to your word." Through Mary's yes, Christ entered the world. Through her faith, she carried our Savior. Through her sorrow, she stood beneath the Cross as Jesus became our Redeemer.

And from that Cross, Jesus gave us something extraordinary. Seeing His mother and the disciple John, He said to Mary, "Woman, behold, your son." Then He said to John, "Behold, your mother." The Church has long understood John to represent more than one disciple standing beneath the Cross. In him, Christ entrusted Mary to His disciples—and His disciples to Mary.

But how do we actually draw close to her? How do we put our hand in the hand of a mother we cannot physically see? For some of us, even the word mother can be complicated. Our relationships with our earthly mothers may have been loving, difficult, imperfect, or some mixture of all three. Our own wounds and insecurities can affect the way we approach Mary. Perhaps we do not need to force that relationship. Perhaps we simply begin by saying, "Mary, I don't completely know how to come close to you. Teach me. Take my hand and bring me to your Son."

The Rosary helps us do exactly that. We repeat the Hail Mary so often that it can become easy to forget how powerful its words are. "Hail Mary, full of grace." These are the words of the angel Gabriel. "Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb." These are the words of Elizabeth. Then comes our request: "Holy Mary, Mother of God, pray for us sinners, now and at the hour of our death."

Now and at the hour of our death. Those words encompass our entire earthly existence. We ask Mary to pray for us now, in whatever we are facing, and someday when our earthly lives come to an end.

Throughout the centuries there have also been reported appearances of Mary. The Church approaches these carefully, and private revelations do not add anything necessary to the Gospel. Yet in the Marian apparitions the Church has recognized, the messages are remarkably consistent: pray, repent, return to God, seek peace, trust Christ, pray for others, and do not despair.

Mary's message ultimately remains the same one she gave at the wedding feast at Cana: "Do whatever He tells you." Perhaps that tells us everything we need to understand about devotion to Mary. She does not ask us to stop at her. She brings us to her Son.

On the Feast of her Assumption, we remember that Mary's life did not end with suffering. The woman who gave her body so that Christ could take on human flesh was brought, body and soul, into heavenly glory. She has already arrived where we hope one day to go. She is the mother who said yes, the mother whose heart was pierced, the mother who remained beneath the Cross, the disciple who believed, the woman full of grace, and the Queen of Heaven and Earth.

Maybe we don't have to understand perfectly how to have a relationship with her. Maybe we simply reach out our hand.

Mary, Mother of Jesus and our Mother, take our hands. Teach us your yes. Teach us to trust when we cannot understand what God is doing. Stay beside us in our sorrow. Pray for us in our weakness. And at the hour of our death, lead us to your Son, so that through Him we may see the Father and enter everlasting life. Amen.
